what_its_for: Faricimab-svoa is used to treat certain eye conditions that can damage your vision. These include wet age-related macular degeneration (wet AMD), diabetic macular edema (DME), macular edema following retinal vein occlusion (RVO), and diabetic retinopathy (DR). These conditions involve abnormal or leaky blood vessels in the back of your eye that can cause blurry vision or vision loss. This medicine helps stop those abnormal blood vessels from growing and leaking, which can protect and sometimes improve your vision.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an injection directly into your eye by a trained eye doctor (ophthalmologist) in a clinic or office setting. You will NOT give this injection to yourself at home. Before the injection, your doctor will numb your eye with eye drops so you feel as little discomfort as possible. The injection is given into the clear, gel-like fluid inside your eye (called the vitreous). Each visit, only one eye is treated at a time. The entire procedure is quick, usually taking just a few minutes. Your eye may feel a little uncomfortable or you may see floaters (tiny spots or shapes) after the injection, but this usually goes away within a day or two.
dosing: Your doctor will decide how often you need injections based on your specific condition and how your eye responds to treatment. In general: For wet AMD and DME, you will usually start with one injection every 4 weeks (monthly) for the first few doses. After that, your doctor may space out your injections to every 8, 12, or even 16 weeks if your condition is stable and responding well to treatment. For RVO, injections are typically given once a month. For diabetic retinopathy, your doctor will create an individualized schedule. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions about how often to come in for your injections.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by your doctor in a clinic, it is very important to keep all of your scheduled appointments. If you have to miss or reschedule an appointment, call your doctor's office as soon as possible to reschedule. Do not skip or delay treatments without talking to your doctor first, as missing doses could allow your eye condition to worsen and may lead to permanent vision loss.
storage: You will not need to store this medicine at home, as it is prepared and given to you by your healthcare provider at the clinic. If for any reason you are provided with the medicine (for example, for a specialty pharmacy arrangement), keep it refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze it. Keep it in its original carton to protect it from light. Do not shake the vial. Keep all medicines out of the reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid rubbing or touching your treated eye after the injection, as this can increase the risk of infection. Avoid swimming or getting water directly in your eye for at least 2 to 3 days after your injection, or as directed by your doctor. Avoid wearing eye makeup until your doctor says it is safe to do so. Do not drive immediately after your injection appointment, as your vision may be temporarily blurry. Have someone available to drive you home. Avoid activities that put pressure on your eye, such as heavy lifting, until your doctor clears you.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your eye doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience any of the following after your injection: sudden increase in eye pain or significant eye discomfort that does not go away, redness in or around your eye that is getting worse, increased sensitivity to light, blurry or decreased vision, or an increase in floaters (spots or dark shapes in your vision). These could be signs of a serious eye infection (endophthalmitis) or other dangerous complications like a retinal detachment or increased pressure in the eye. Also contact your doctor if you have signs of a stroke or heart attack such as sudden numbness or weakness on one side of the body, sudden confusion, trouble speaking, chest pain, or shortness of breath, as faricimab-svoa may rarely be associated with these events.
when_it_works: Many patients begin to see improvement in their vision within the first 1 to 3 months of starting treatment, but results vary from person to person. Some people may notice stabilization of their vision (meaning it stops getting worse) rather than immediate improvement. It is important to continue your treatments as scheduled even if your vision seems stable, because stopping too soon can allow the disease to come back. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular eye exams and imaging tests.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: It is not known if faricimab-svoa can harm an unborn baby or pass into breast milk. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 3 months after the last injection. Older adults: This medicine is most commonly used in older adults and has been studied in this group. No special dose adjustments are needed based on age alone. Kidney or liver disease: No dose adjustments are currently required for patients with kidney or liver problems, but always tell your doctor about all of your medical conditions. Children: The safety and effectiveness of faricimab-svoa in children have not been established.
